blocks.source: Vol IV, Trajectory Planning, § Kinodynamic Feasibility
blocks.md: A candidate trajectory that clears every obstacle in workspace and arrives before its deadline will still fault on the hardware if it asks a joint for more speed, torque, or current slew than the drive can supply. What an embodied model generates is a geometric and timed proposal, not permission to move. While high-level motion planners and learned policies navigate free configuration space FreeConfigurationSpace, physical actuators operate under fixed electromotive, thermal, and structural limits.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why C2 seam matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Splicing chunks that match only position or velocity leaves an acceleration step that reflected inertia turns into a torque step, so seams must be C2 and the replacement is planned from the projected seam state.

questions.q: The section **Kinodynamic Feasibility** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Splicing chunks that match only position or velocity leaves an acceleration step that reflected inertia turns into a torque step, so seams must be C2 and the replacement is planned from the projected seam state.

Clearance and tool limits live in tool space but drives enforce joint limits, so tool-space quantities pass through the configuration-dependent Jacobian, whose weak direction near a singularity demands unbounded joint rates unless damped least squares trades accuracy for bounded rates.

Replacement latency runs from capture to MCU admission (about 115 ms against a 50 ms renewal and a 60 ms lease), so renewal is sustainable only by overlapping requests and every record must carry its own handoff tail.

The planner hands over an immutable record naming frame, evidence epoch, seam state, parent intent-lease digest, and four MCU-clock deadlines in two tiers (high-rate chunk lease, hardware commitment cutoff) together with its latched stop.
